newsitem.title: GERMANY: German states mull surveillance for Scientology.
newsitem.headline: German states mull surveillance for Scientology.

text.p: Leaders of Germany's 16 regional states said on Friday they wanted to study whether the Church of Scientology should be placed under surveillance by the government's anti-extremist watchdog.

State premiers also said at the end of a two-day conference in the eastern city of Erfurt they would ask the federal government to set up a central coordination office to gather information about Scientology.

The Church of Scientology said the states' proposals were chilling. "It is astonishing and frightening to see how the states are trampling on basic human rights," said Franz Riedl, a spokesman for the Scientologists in Hamburg.
"Some of these politicians are fanatical extremists and they have created an atmosphere of hysteria," he added. "Surveillance is only the first step. They want more state and fewer rights."
The premiers asked their interior ministries to explore whether the organisation should be monitored by the anti-extremist Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution.
Two southern states, Bavaria and Baden-Wuerttemberg, said they also wanted the ministries to consider enacting a nationwide ban on Scientology members from public service.
The sect says it has around 30,000 German members. The government puts the real figure at between 10,000 and 20,000.

Scientology, founded in 1954 by American science fiction writer L. Ron Hubbard, gives would-be members personality tests and then offers courses and literature to help them realise what the church sees as their full potential.

Germany has stricter regulations on church status than the United States and has refused to register Scientology as a religion. Some officials see it as a totalitarian group using manipulative practices for profit.
Because of its own Nazi past, Germany tends to take a tough stand on groups it thinks threaten its postwar democracy.

The youth wing of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling Christian Democratic (CDU) called earlier this year for a boycott of the Hollywood blockbuster "Mission:Impossible" because it stars Tom Cruise -- one of several high-profile Scientologists.
Scientology last week blasted recent moves to limit its activities in Germany, saying in an advertisement in the New York Times that Bonn used Nazi-style tactics against it.
Bonn rejected that charge as absurd and said it insulted the millions of Jewish victims of the Nazi Holocaust.
